lesson_title: One Tournament, Two Kitchens, Three Economic Systems
hook_text: A sold-out amagwinya table just explained capitalism better than any textbook.
clip_script: Picture a Saturday sports tournament: eight teams, a crowd of families, everybody hungry. Somebody has to answer three questions before noon. What food gets made? How? And who gets fed? Answer one lives at the food stalls along the fence. Nobody organised them. The amagwinya stand sells out before the first whistle; the fruit-cup stand barely moves. Nobody calls a meeting — next Saturday there are two amagwinya stands. The sold-out table sent the message and the pricing did the planning. Spectators with cash eat lekker; the kid without coins just smells the oil. That is the free market. Answer two lives in the organisers' tent. One committee, one giant pot of curry, every player fed free. Nobody plays hungry. But if half the players hate curry, they eat curry anyway, every tournament — no till exists to overrule the committee. Fairer plates, blinder cooking. And answer three is what the tournament actually does: the free meal tent AND the stalls, both at once. That is a mixed economy. That is South Africa, in one sports ground.
visual_style: A sunny community sports ground drawn in bold flat colour: a fence line of food stalls with hand-painted price boards, a big canvas tent with one steaming pot, a scoreboard flipping between WHAT, HOW and FOR WHOM.
mood: Playful and familiar, sharpening into something serious.
pacing: Three quick kitchen beats, one slow beat on the kid at the fence, decisive final line.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and learn to classify any economy on earth in three sentences.
